title: GuidanceNFT: NFT-Based Reward Fine-Tuning of Guided Diffusion Models

paper.title: GuidanceNFT: NFT-Based Reward Fine-Tuning of Guided Diffusion Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract DiffusionNFT (NFT) fine-tunes diffusion models toward task-specific rewards,
but optimizing these rewards does not guarantee fidelity to the full prompt.
Although classifier-free guidance (CFG) strengthens prompt alignment, NFT is
formulated as a CFG-free method, and applying CFG to the fine-tuned velocity
field can reduce the optimized reward. This motivates optimizing rewards over
the guided output distribution while seeking to retain its prompt alignment.
However, applying standard NFT directly to guided samples can cause reward
degradation or training collapse. We trace this failure to a mismatch between
the reference velocity used in the NFT loss and the score of the guided sample
distribution, which biases the improvement direction. We propose GuidanceNFT,
which estimates the matching reference velocity through online flow matching
on guided samples and uses it to correct both regression terms. With an exact
reference, the corrected objective recovers NFT’s intended update. In our
experiments, the learned correction sustains reward improvement under both
explicit and built-in guidance. On SD3.5-M, GuidanceNFT achieves higher
optimized rewards than NFT with and without CFG across GenEval,
text-rendering, and multi-reward objectives, together with better overall
prompt alignment as measured by off-domain evaluation metrics. Experiments on
models with built-in guidance, including Model Guidance and ELF, further
demonstrate improved ImageNet generation, a better perplexity–entropy
tradeoff on OpenWebText, and higher accuracy on GSM8K.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reward fine-tuning adapts pretrained diffusion models to task-specific objectives. DiffusionNFT (NFT) ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) is a recent and efficient approach that fine-tunes models through forward-process regression by contrasting high- and low-reward generations, requiring neither reward gradients nor trajectory likelihoods. While classifier-free guidance (CFG) strengthens prompt alignment by combining conditional and empty-condition predictions ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) , NFT is formulated as a CFG-free method that, without CFG, exceeds the task rewards of CFG-based fine-tuning such as Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . However, optimizing a task reward does not guarantee fidelity to the full prompt: an OCR-specialized NFT model can render the requested words while omitting the surrounding scene (Figure 4 ). Applying CFG to the fine-tuned velocity field does not necessarily restore prompt alignment and, in our SD3.5-M experiments, even reduces the optimized reward for all three training objectives. This tension motivates applying NFT to improve a guided velocity field with stronger prompt alignment, allowing reward optimization to start from the generation behavior we intend to retain (Figure 1 ). This approach could also extend NFT to models with built-in guidance , whose native predictions are already guided. NFT appears well suited to this setting because it derives an improvement direction from the contrast between positive and negative samples without relying on the internal sampling trajectory. However, we observe reward degradation or training collapse when applying the standard NFT objective directly to guided samples (Figures 3 and 5 ). We trace this failure to the reference velocity in the NFT loss. NFT obtains its improvement direction from a regression loss built on velocity targets for re-noised samples and their corresponding rewards. To recover the direction suggested by the positive–negative contrast, it relies on a shared reference velocity that is collinear with the positive and negative conditional mean velocities. The original or guided sampling field, however, need not preserve this property (Section 3 ). We show that a mismatch in the reference velocity can introduce a bias that rotates the intended update. We therefore propose GuidanceNFT , which estimates the required reference velocity through flow matching on guided samples. This reference turns out to correspond to the conditional score of the rollout distribution. We use it to correct the NFT objective, which then recovers NFT’s intended reward-driven update to the model’s velocity field. In our experiments, this correction prevents the collapse observed with standard NFT and sustains reward improvement. GuidanceNFT improves both task reward and prompt alignment in our experiments. On SD3.5-M, it achieves higher optimized rewards than NFT with and without CFG across GenEval, text-rendering, and multi-reward objectives, together with better overall prompt alignment as measured by off-domain evaluation metrics. On models with built-in guidance, GuidanceNFT improves ImageNet generation with Model Guidance and achieves a better perplexity–entropy tradeoff on OpenWebText with ELF-B. On the Qwen-based ELF reasoning model, it outperforms NFT’s best retained checkpoint at every reported Pass@ k k on GSM8K. Our main contributions are: 1. Integrating NFT with guidance. We apply NFT to guided velocity fields and identify the collinear reference velocity required by its regression objective. Our analysis and experiments link a biased reference to reward degradation and training collapse across multiple settings. 2. Enabling NFT to tilt guided distributions toward higher rewards. We introduce GuidanceNFT, which estimates the required reference velocity through flow matching on guided samples and uses it to correct the NFT objective. This correction enables sustained reward improvement in settings where standard NFT degrades or collapses. 3. Improved task performance and broader alignment. GuidanceNFT builds on the prompt alignment of guided velocity fields to achieve higher optimized rewards on SD3.5-M, together with better overall prompt alignment as measured by off-domain evaluation metrics. Experiments with Model Guidance and self-conditioning CFG further show improved ImageNet generation, a better perplexity–entropy tradeoff on OpenWebText, and higher accuracy on GSM8K.

sections.heading: 2 Background
sections.text: We review the regression objective used by NFT and the explicit and built-in guidance mechanisms that determine the rollout distributions in this work.

sections.heading: 2.1 DiffusionNFT: Reward Feedback Through a Shared Reference
sections.text: DiffusionNFT (NFT) ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) fine-tunes a diffusion model using generated samples and their rewards, without requiring reward gradients or trajectory likelihoods. Given an endpoint distribution q ( ⋅ ∣ c ) q(\cdot\mid c) and processed reward weights r ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] r\in[0,1] , it defines positive and negative populations q + ∝ r ​ q q^{+}\propto rq and q − ∝ ( 1 − r ) ​ q q^{-}\propto(1-r)q . The positive population places greater weight on higher-reward samples, motivating an update toward this distribution. NFT implements this distributional update through the velocity field. Generated endpoints are re-noised to estimate the velocity fields associated with the positive and negative populations. The difference between these fields provides a local improvement direction for the velocity field of the original, untilted distribution. Rather than fitting the two targets with separate models, NFT trains a single policy v θ v_{\theta} against a frozen copy v old v^{\rm old} of the policy that generated the samples. For β > 0 \beta>0 , it minimizes ℒ NFT ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ r ​ ‖ β ​ v θ + ( 1 − β ) ​ v old − v ‖ 2 + ( 1 − r ) ​ ‖ ( 1 + β ) ​ v old − β ​ v θ − v ‖ 2 ] , \mathcal{L}_{\rm NFT}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[r\,\big\|\beta v_{\theta}+(1-\beta)v^{\rm old}-v\big\|^{2}+(1-r)\,\big\|(1+\beta)v^{\rm old}-\beta v_{\theta}-v\big\|^{2}\right], (1) where x t x_{t} is a generated endpoint x x re-noised to time t t , v v is its sample velocity, and both terms are evaluated at the same state ( x t , c , t ) (x_{t},c,t) . The frozen policy v old v^{\rm old} serves as the shared reference for the positive and negative terms (Section 3 ). This objective uses reward feedback to move the policy toward the positive population without requiring the sampling trajectories.

sections.heading: Classifier-free guidance.
sections.text: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) strengthens conditioning by extrapolating from the empty-condition prediction v ∅ v_{\varnothing} toward the conditional prediction v c v_{c} ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) : v w = v ∅ + w ⁡ ( v c − v ∅ ) = w ​ v c + ( 1 − w ) ​ v ∅ . v_{w}=v_{\varnothing}+w(v_{c}-v_{\varnothing})=wv_{c}+(1-w)v_{\varnothing}. (2) Here w = 1 w=1 gives conditional-only sampling, whereas w > 1 w>1 amplifies the difference between the two predictions. We refer to this as explicit guidance: it is applied at sampling time, requires two model evaluations per step, and can be removed by setting w = 1 w=1 .

sections.heading: Model Guidance.
sections.text: Guidance can also be built into the model’s native prediction. Model Guidance (MG) ( Tang et al., 2025 ) trains the conditional prediction M c M_{c} , in velocity coordinates, toward v + λ ​ sg ⁡ ( M c − M ∅ ) v+\lambda\operatorname{sg}(M_{c}-M_{\varnothing}) , where sg \operatorname{sg} denotes stop-gradient. For a fixed 0 ≤ λ < 1 0\leq\lambda<1 , the ideal fixed point has the CFG form M c = w eff ​ C data + ( 1 − w eff ) ​ M ∅ , w eff = 1 / ( 1 − λ ) , M_{c}=w_{\rm eff}C_{\rm data}+(1-w_{\rm eff})M_{\varnothing},\qquad w_{\rm eff}=1/(1-\lambda), (3) where C data C_{\rm data} is the unweighted conditional mean velocity of the pretraining data. The native prediction M c M_{c} is therefore already a guided field and requires one model evaluation per inference step. We call this built-in guidance: it is fixed during pretraining, so there is no sampling-time guidance scale that can be set to one to recover conditional-only sampling.

sections.heading: Self-conditioning CFG (SCCFG).
sections.text: ELF ( Hu et al., 2026 ) incorporates guidance through its own clean-embedding prediction. The same network produces a self-conditioned field S θ w S_{\theta}^{w} and a field S θ , ∅ w S_{\theta,\varnothing}^{w} with zero self-conditioning input; both retain any task prompt. The self-conditioning input comes from a detached initial prediction during training and from the preceding sampling step during inference. The training target is v target = v + ( 1 − 1 / w ) ​ sg ⁡ ( S θ w − S θ , ∅ w ) . v_{\rm target}=v+\left(1-1/w\right)\operatorname{sg}(S_{\theta}^{w}-S_{\theta,\varnothing}^{w}). (4) As with MG, the self-conditioned prediction used for sampling is itself a guided field. Explicit CFG, MG, and SCCFG all produce guided predictions that typically improve sample quality or prompt alignment relative to the unguided conditional prediction. This motivates applying NFT directly to guided predictions. Standard NFT, however, is formulated for conditional-only rollouts ( w = 1 w=1 ) and does not cover built-in guidance. Section 3 presents GuidanceNFT, which extends NFT to guided samples under both explicit and built-in guidance.

sections.heading: 3 GuidanceNFT
sections.text: GuidanceNFT adapts NFT to guided samples by correcting its reference velocity. We first express the reward-driven update in terms of the positive and negative velocity fields and identify the reference that aligns both regression terms with this update. We then relate this reference to the score of the re-noised rollout distribution, examine the bias introduced by an inaccurate reference, and estimate the required reference through online flow matching.

sections.heading: 3.2 Reference Mismatch Under Guidance
sections.text: When a model’s velocity matches the conditional mean velocity of its re-noised rollout distribution, the required reference is available directly from the model. Standard NFT uses the frozen prediction v old v^{\rm old} as this reference. For guided rollouts, however, the conditional prediction v c v_{c} alone generally does not represent v ¯ q CFG \bar{v}_{q_{\rm CFG}} . Analyses of CFG distinguish its sampling distribution from the density suggested by the instantaneous guided score ( Bradley & Nakkiran, 2025 ) . Thus neither v c v_{c} nor v w v_{w} is guaranteed to supply the required reference; Appendix A.2 details this distinction. Figure 2: Reference error distorts the reward-driven update. (a) A matched reference spreads samples across the rewarded branches through the intended update in (b). (c) An incorrect reference concentrates samples on fewer branches. (d) The reference error adds a displacement that (e), applied alone, moves samples away from the reward target. Hit reports the fraction reaching the reward target and cells the spatial diversity. In the observed training runs, larger reference gaps accompany faster reward collapse (Figure 3 ), consistent with the effect of reference error in Equation 10 . sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: Our experiments test whether correcting NFT’s reference velocity enables reward fine-tuning to improve guided models while retaining prompt alignment and generation quality. We first examine training dynamics and reward specialization under explicit CFG, then evaluate models with built-in guidance on ImageNet generation, OpenWebText ( Gokaslan et al., 2019 ) language modeling, and GSM8K reasoning. Training and evaluation protocols, uncertainty estimates, and costs are given in Appendices C and E .

GuidanceNFT achieves higher optimized rewards than NFT both with and without CFG, and leads on all seven evaluation metrics for GenEval and OCR specialization. For Learned3, it achieves the highest composite reward together with strong preference and alignment scores. This overall performance supports reward fine-tuning that retains the prompt alignment of guided generation. OCR illustrates how task reward and broader prompt alignment can improve together. NFT without CFG attains an OCR reward of 0.971 but a held-out GenEval score of only 0.035. GuidanceNFT raises the OCR reward to 0.975 and reaches 0.488 on GenEval. The selected examples in Figure 4 (last four columns) show readable text within the requested scenes, including a watch on a wrist and a sign on a mountain summit. These results indicate that accurate text rendering can coexist with substantially better compositional alignment than standard NFT achieves. For Learned3, GuidanceNFT attains a composite reward of 1.528, compared with 1.519 for NFT without CFG and 1.495 for NFT with CFG. It also improves OCR, CLIPScore, Aesthetic ( Schuhmann et al., 2022 ) , and ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) over both NFT variants. The selected examples in Figure 4 (first four columns) illustrate retention of requested content, including a portrait within a triangular frame and an umbrella resting on a spoon. Although the gains are not uniform across metrics, these results show that Learned3 optimization can improve reward while retaining image quality and prompt alignment. sections.heading: 4.2 Built-in Guidance: Reward Optimization of Native Guided Fields
sections.text: Model Guidance (MG) ( Tang et al., 2025 ) and ELF self-conditioning guidance ( Hu et al., 2026 ) incorporate guidance into their native predictions. We test whether estimating the reference from each model’s own rollouts also improves reward fine-tuning in these settings. Sustained improvement in image generation. On MG, GuidanceNFT continues to improve ImageNet reward as standard NFT peaks and then declines (Figure 5 (a)). Its selected checkpoint reaches a PickScore of 21.580, compared with 20.010 for NFT’s best retained checkpoint (Appendix F ). The selected MG examples in Figure 6 (b) show clearer object details, including the snowmobile body and the bighorn’s curved horns. Together with the SiT results in Section 4.1 , these findings support reference correction for ImageNet reward fine-tuning under both explicit and built-in guidance. sections.heading: 5 Related Work
sections.text: Reward fine-tuning through regression. DDPO ( Black et al., 2024 ) and Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) optimize rewards through trajectory policy gradients. DiffusionNFT ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) instead contrasts rewarded endpoints through forward-process regression. Reward Score Matching ( Lee et al., 2026 ) , AdvantageFlow ( Kveton et al., 2026 ) , and Reinforce Adjoint Matching ( Bergmeister et al., 2026 ) also connect reward optimization to regression. Reward-based velocity matching (RVM) ( Choi et al., 2026 ) recovers NFT through reward weights and anchor choices. We identify the reference that aligns NFT’s positive and negative feedback on guided samples, and show how reference error biases the update. Guidance and the rollout distribution. CFG ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) strengthens conditioning through extrapolated predictions; Model Guidance ( Tang et al., 2025 ) and ELF ( Hu et al., 2026 ) incorporate guidance into the native field. Guidance analyses distinguish the sampler’s distribution from the density suggested by its instantaneous score ( Bradley & Nakkiran, 2025 ; Chidambaram et al., 2024 ; Jiang & Ma, 2026 ) . NFT requires the conditional mean velocity of re-noised endpoints, which need not equal the sampling field. The SCCFG-compatible NFT adaptation of Cheng (2026) , denoted CEDR in our experiments, algebraically reconstructs a base prediction. GuidanceNFT instead fits the reference to the current rollout population, covering both explicit and built-in guidance. Estimating a reference from generated samples. Generated-distribution estimators appear in variational score distillation ( Wang et al., 2023 ) and distribution matching distillation (DMD) ( Yin et al., 2024b ) ; DMD2 ( Yin et al., 2024a ) links inaccurate estimation to training instability. GuidanceNFT uses flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) on unweighted guided endpoints to estimate the shared reference for NFT’s two regressions. Where guided distillation ( Meng et al., 2023 ) and rectified flow ( Liu et al., 2023 ) train sampling fields, our auxiliary fit calibrates the reward update. Online fitting adds training cost but no inference passes. Preserving quality beyond the optimized reward. Pretrained empty-condition predictions can retain generation quality after fine-tuning ( Phunyaphibarn et al., 2026 ) . Centered Reward Distillation ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) controls drift through within-prompt reward centering and a guided pretrained reference; ReNFT ( Bao et al., 2026 ) repairs diversity collapse after reward training. We correct NFT’s velocity reference during training, a different role from reward centering or pretrained regularization. Our evaluations examine prompt alignment and text diversity alongside task reward.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: NFT requires a reference velocity that matches its rollout distribution. Under guidance, a reference gap adds a component to the reward-driven update, which explains why matching sampling and training guidance alone is insufficient. GuidanceNFT estimates the reference online with flow matching and applies a shared correction to NFT’s positive and negative regressions. Across explicit and built-in guidance, it prevents the degradation observed with NFT and improves reward optimization, image quality, and language generation without additional inference passes.

sections.text: Equation 10 predicts that an inaccurate reference adds the displacement ( 1 − 2 ​ α ) ​ e (1-2\alpha)e to the intended update Δ \Delta . sections.text: The reference comparison uses five rollout steps, 512 × 512 512\times 512 resolution, 48 prompt groups with 24 images each, one policy update per iteration, β = 1 \beta=1 , and regularization coefficient 10 − 4 10^{-4} . sections.heading: Reward and loss conventions.
sections.text: PickScore/Pick-a-Pic ( Kirstain et al., 2023 ) , HPSv2 ( Wu et al., 2023 ) , and ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) provide learned preference scores. HPS uses the v2.1 checkpoint. The CLIPScore column follows NFT’s scorer: the paired image–text logit divided by 100, with CLIP ViT-L/14 ( Radford et al., 2021 ) as its source-code default. It is not the original rescaled CLIPScore definition of Hessel et al. (2021) . SD3.5 uses AdamW with learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , coefficients ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) (0.9,0.999) , weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} , and gradient clipping at 1. Training uses FP16, two H200 GPUs, and LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) ; the retained Learned3 checkpoint specifies rank 32, scaling parameter 64, and dropout 0. The conditional microbatch is 24 per GPU with accumulation 24. The sampler is deterministic DPM2. Following the NFT implementation, training uses a fraction 0.99 of the rollout time grid. Let s i s_{i} be the summed raw task score, s ¯ c i \bar{s}_{c_{i}} its prompt-group mean in the current collected batch, and σ B \sigma_{B} the standard deviation across that batch. The SD3.5 reward mapping is A i = s i − s ¯ c i σ B + 10 − 4 , R i = 1 2 + clip ⁡ ( A i , − 5 , 5 ) 10 . A_{i}=\frac{s_{i}-\bar{s}_{c_{i}}}{\sigma_{B}+10^{-4}},\qquad R_{i}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{clip}(A_{i},-5,5)}{10}. (31) Prompt statistics are cleared after each outer update. The NFT branch losses receive weights R i R_{i} and 1 − R i 1-R_{i} , with an overall multiplier 5 / β 5/\beta . In clean-sample prediction space, a velocity residual is multiplied by the noise time. Its squared residual is divided by its detached per-example mean absolute residual, lower-bounded by 10 − 5 10^{-5} . The regularization term penalizes the deviation of the policy prediction from that of a frozen copy of the model. These adaptive denominators and regularizers follow the NFT implementation. Held-out GenEval aggregates retain all valid rewards, including the minimum value − 10 -10 . The online reward curve in Figure 3 (b) excludes samples with reward − 10 -10 , whereas the advantage calculation during training uses all rewards.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.15856v1 [cs.LG] 11 Oct 2026 GuidanceNFT: NFT-Based Reward Fine-Tuning of Guided Diffusion Models Jiayin Liu Affiliation: Tsinghua University Zeyu Michael Li Affiliation: Duke University Bingshuo Qian Affiliation: Duke University Xiang Cheng Affiliation: Duke University Abstract DiffusionNFT (NFT) fine-tunes diffusion models toward task-specific rewards, but optimizing these rewards does not guarantee fidelity to the full prompt. Although classifier-free guidance (CFG) strengthens prompt alignment, NFT is formulated as a CFG-free method, and applying CFG to the fine-tuned velocity field can reduce the optimized reward. This motivates optimizing rewards over the guided output distribution while seeking to retain its prompt alignment. However, applying standard NFT directly to guided samples can cause reward degradation or training collapse. We trace this failure to a mismatch between the reference velocity used in the NFT loss and the score of the guided sample distribution, which biases the improvement direction. We propose GuidanceNFT, which estimates the matching reference velocity through online flow matching on guided samples and uses it to correct both regression terms. With an exact reference, the corrected objective recovers NFT’s intended update. In our experiments, the learned correction sustains reward improvement under both explicit and built-in guidance. On SD3.5-M, GuidanceNFT achieves higher optimized rewards than NFT with and without CFG across GenEval, text-rendering, and multi-reward objectives, together with better overall prompt alignment as measured by off-domain evaluation metrics. Experiments on models with built-in guidance, including Model Guidance and ELF, further demonstrate improved ImageNet generation, a better perplexity–entropy tradeoff on OpenWebText, and higher accuracy on GSM8K. † † footnotetext: Emails: jiayin-l23@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn ; {zeyu.li030, bingshuo.qian, xiang.cheng}@duke.edu . Figure 1: Updating the guided field improves reward while retaining data structure. (a–b) Pretrained samples without and with CFG. (c) NFT moves samples toward the rewarded branches, but (d) adding CFG afterward pushes many samples off the tree. (e) Updating the guided field better combines reward targeting with tree fidelity. Panels (c–e) zoom into the dashed region; blue branches mark the reward target and orange points mark off-tree samples. 1 Introduction Reward fine-tuning adapts pretrained diffusion models to task-specific objectives. DiffusionNFT (NFT) ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) is a recent and efficient approach that fine-tunes models through forward-process regression by contrasting high- and low-reward generations, requiring neither reward gradients nor trajectory likelihoods. While classifier-free guidance (CFG) strengthens prompt alignment by combining conditional and empty-condition predictions ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) , NFT is formulated as a CFG-free method that, without CFG, exceeds the task rewards of CFG-based fine-tuning such as Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . However, optimizing a task reward does not guarantee fidelity to the full prompt: an OCR-specialized NFT model can render the requested words while omitting the surrounding scene (Figure 4 ). Applying CFG to the fine-tuned velocity field does not necessarily restore prompt alignment and, in our SD3.5-M experiments, even reduces the optimized reward for all three training objectives. This tension motivates applying NFT to improve a guided velocity field with stronger prompt alignment, allowing reward optimization to start from the generation behavior we intend to retain (Figure 1 ). This approach could also extend NFT to models with built-in guidance , whose native predictions are already guided. NFT appears well suited to this setting because it derives an improvement direction from the contrast between positive and negative samples without relying on the internal sampling trajectory. However, we observe reward degradation or training collapse when applying the standard NFT objective directly to guided samples (Figures 3 and 5 ). We trace this failure to the reference velocity in the NFT loss. NFT obtains its improvement direction from a regression loss built on velocity targets for re-noised samples and their corresponding rewards. To recover the direction suggested by the positive–negative contrast, it relies on a shared reference velocity that is collinear with the positive and negative conditional mean velocities. The original or guided sampling field, however, need not preserve this property (Section 3 ). We show that a mismatch in the reference velocity can introduce a bias that rotates the intended update. We therefore propose GuidanceNFT , which estimates the required reference velocity through flow matching on guided samples. This reference turns out to correspond to the conditional score of the rollout distribution. We use it to correct the NFT objective, which then recovers NFT’s intended reward-driven update to the model’s velocity field. In our experiments, this correction prevents the collapse observed with standard NFT and sustains reward improvement. GuidanceNFT improves both task reward and prompt alignment in our experiments. On SD3.5-M, it achieves higher optimized rewards than NFT with and without CFG across GenEval, text-rendering, and multi-reward objectives, together with better overall prompt alignment as measured by off-domain evaluation metrics. On models with built-in guidance, GuidanceNFT improves ImageNet generation with Model Guidance and achieves a better perplexity–entropy tradeoff on OpenWebText with ELF-B. On the Qwen-based ELF reasoning model, it outperforms NFT’s best retained checkpoint at every reported Pass@ k k on GSM8K. Our main contributions are: 1. Integrating NFT with guidance. We apply NFT to guided velocity fields and identify the collinear reference velocity required by its regression objective. Our analysis and experiments link a biased reference to reward degradation and training collapse across multiple settings. 2. Enabling NFT to tilt guided distributions toward higher rewards. We introduce GuidanceNFT, which estimates the required reference velocity through flow matching on guided samples and uses it to correct the NFT objective. This correction enables sustained reward improvement in settings where standard NFT degrades or collapses. 3. Improved task performance and broader alignment. GuidanceNFT builds on the prompt alignment of guided velocity fields to achieve higher optimized rewards on SD3.5-M, together with better overall prompt alignment as measured by off-domain evaluation metrics. Experiments with Model Guidance and self-conditioning CFG further show improved ImageNet generation, a better perplexity–entropy tradeoff on OpenWebText, and higher accuracy on GSM8K. 2 Background We review the regression objective used by NFT and the explicit and built-in guidance mechanisms that determine the rollout distributions in this work. 2.1 DiffusionNFT: Reward Feedback Through a Shared Reference DiffusionNFT (NFT) ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) fine-tunes a diffusion model using generated samples and their rewards, without requiring reward gradients or trajectory likelihoods. Given an endpoint distribution q ( ⋅ ∣ c ) q(\cdot\mid c) and processed reward weights r ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] r\in[0,1] , it defines positive and negative populations q + ∝ r ​ q q^{+}\propto rq and q − ∝ ( 1 − r ) ​ q q^{-}\propto(1-r)q . The positive population places greater weight on higher-reward samples, motivating an update toward this distribution. NFT implements this distributional update through the velocity field. Generated endpoints are re-noised to estimate the velocity fields associated with the positive and negative populations. The difference between these fields provides a local improvement direction for the velocity field of the original, untilted distribution. Rather than fitting the two targets with separate models, NFT trains a single policy v θ v_{\theta} against a frozen copy v old v^{\rm old} of the policy that generated the samples. For β > 0 \beta>0 , it minimizes ℒ NFT ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ r ​ ‖ β ​ v θ + ( 1 − β ) ​ v old − v ‖ 2 + ( 1 − r ) ​ ‖ ( 1 + β ) ​ v old − β ​ v θ − v ‖ 2 ] , \mathcal{L}_{\rm NFT}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\left[r\,\big\|\beta v_{\theta}+(1-\beta)v^{\rm old}-v\big\|^{2}+(1-r)\,\big\|(1+\beta)v^{\rm old}-\beta v_{\theta}-v\big\|^{2}\right], (1) where x t x_{t} is a generated endpoint x x re-noised to time t t , v v is its sample velocity, and both terms are evaluated at the same state ( x t , c , t ) (x_{t},c,t) . The frozen policy v old v^{\rm old} serves as the shared reference for the positive and negative terms (Section 3 ). This objective uses reward feedback to move the policy toward the positive population without requiring the sampling trajectories. 2.2 Explicit and Built-in Guidance Classifier-free guidance. Classifier-free guidance (CFG) strengthens conditioning by extrapolating from the empty-condition prediction v ∅ v_{\varnothing} toward the conditional prediction v c v_{c} ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) : v w = v ∅ + w ⁡ ( v c − v ∅ ) = w ​ v c + ( 1 − w ) ​ v ∅ . v_{w}=v_{\varnothing}+w(v_{c}-v_{\varnothing})=wv_{c}+(1-w)v_{\varnothing}. (2) Here w = 1 w=1 gives conditional-only sampling, whereas w > 1 w>1 amplifies the difference between the two predictions. We refer to this as explicit guidance: it is applied at sampling time, requires two model evaluations per step, and can be removed by setting w = 1 w=1 . Model Guidance. Guidance can also be built into the model’s native prediction. Model Guidance (MG) ( Tang et al., 2025 ) trains the conditional prediction M c M_{c} , in velocity coordinates, toward v + λ ​ sg ⁡ ( M c − M ∅ ) v+\lambda\operatorname{sg}(M_{c}-M_{\varnothing}) , where sg \operatorname{sg} denotes stop-gradient. For a fixed 0 ≤ λ < 1 0\leq\lambda<1 , the ideal fixed point has the CFG form M c = w eff ​ C data + ( 1 − w eff ) ​ M ∅ , w eff = 1 / ( 1 − λ ) , M_{c}=w_{\rm eff}C_{\rm data}+(1-w_{\rm eff})M_{\varnothing},\qquad w_{\rm eff}=1/(1-\lambda), (3) where C data C_{\rm data} is the unweighted conditional mean velocity of the pretraining data. The native prediction M c M_{c} is therefore already a guided field and requires one model evaluation per inference step. We call this built-in guidance: it is fixed during pretraining, so there is no sampling-time guidance scale that can be set to one to recover conditional-only sampling. Self-conditioning CFG (SCCFG). ELF ( Hu et al., 2026 ) incorporates guidance through its own clean-embedding prediction. The same network produces a self-conditioned field S θ w S_{\theta}^{w} and a field S θ , ∅ w S_{\theta,\varnothing}^{w} with zero self-conditioning input; both retain any task prompt. The self-conditioning input comes from a detached initial prediction during training and from the preceding sampling step during inference. The training target is v target = v + ( 1 − 1 / w ) ​ sg ⁡ ( S θ w − S θ , ∅ w ) . v_{\rm target}=v+\left(1-1/w\right)\operatorname{sg}(S_{\theta}^{w}-S_{\theta,\varnothing}^{w}). Explicit CFG, MG, and SCCFG all produce guided predictions that typically improve sample quality or prompt alignment relative to the unguided conditional prediction. DDPO ( Black et al., 2024 ) and Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) optimize rewards through trajectory policy gradients. DiffusionNFT ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) instead contrasts rewarded endpoints through forward-process regression. Reward Score Matching ( Lee et al., 2026 ) , AdvantageFlow ( Kveton et al., 2026 ) , and Reinforce Adjoint Matching ( Bergmeister et al., 2026 ) also connect reward optimization to regression. Reward-based velocity matching (RVM) ( Choi et al., 2026 ) recovers NFT through reward weights and anchor choices. We identify the reference that aligns NFT’s positive and negative feedback on guided samples, and show how reference error biases the update. Guidance and the rollout distribution. CFG ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) strengthens conditioning through extrapolated predictions; Model Guidance ( Tang et al., 2025 ) and ELF ( Hu et al., 2026 ) incorporate guidance into the native field. Guidance analyses distinguish the sampler’s distribution from the density suggested by its instantaneous score ( Bradley & Nakkiran, 2025 ; Chidambaram et al., 2024 ; Jiang & Ma, 2026 ) . NFT requires the conditional mean velocity of re-noised endpoints, which need not equal the sampling field. The SCCFG-compatible NFT adaptation of Cheng (2026) , denoted CEDR in our experiments, algebraically reconstructs a base prediction. GuidanceNFT instead fits the reference to the current rollout population, covering both explicit and built-in guidance. Estimating a reference from generated samples. Generated-distribution estimators appear in variational score distillation ( Wang et al., 2023 ) and distribution matching distillation (DMD) ( Yin et al., 2024b ) ; DMD2 ( Yin et al., 2024a ) links inaccurate estimation to training instability. GuidanceNFT uses flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) on unweighted guided endpoints to estimate the shared reference for NFT’s two regressions. Where guided distillation ( Meng et al., 2023 ) and rectified flow ( Liu et al., 2023 ) train sampling fields, our auxiliary fit calibrates the reward update. Online fitting adds training cost but no inference passes. Preserving quality beyond the optimized reward. Pretrained empty-condition predictions can retain generation quality after fine-tuning ( Phunyaphibarn et al., 2026 ) . Centered Reward Distillation ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) controls drift through within-prompt reward centering and a guided pretrained reference; ReNFT ( Bao et al., 2026 ) repairs diversity collapse after reward training. We correct NFT’s velocity reference during training, a different role from reward centering or pretrained regularization. Our evaluations examine prompt alignment and text diversity alongside task reward. 6 Conclusion NFT requires a reference velocity that matches its rollout distribution. Under guidance, a reference gap adds a component to the reward-driven update, which explains why matching sampling and training guidance alone is insufficient. GuidanceNFT estimates the reference online with flow matching and applies a shared correction to NFT’s positive and negative regressions. Across explicit and built-in guidance, it prevents the degradation observed with NFT and improves reward optimization, image quality, and language generation without additional inference passes.
